units.title: Chemical Bonding and Forces of Attraction
units.intro: Atoms stick because electrons are shared or transferred.

cards.title: 2.1 Forces of Attractions
body: **Chemical bonds** are the forces of attraction that hold atoms together: can be described as attractive forces.
Intramolecular bonds refer to the forces of attraction that hold atoms together within a molecule.
Generally, intramolecular forces are considerably stronger than intermolecular forces.

cards.title: Step by step: Forces of attraction
body: **Step 1:** Intramolecular forces (chemical bonds) hold atoms together inside a substance: ionic (transfer of electrons, metal + non-metal), covalent (sharing of electron pairs, non-metals) and metallic (cations in a sea of delocalized electrons).
**Step 2:** Intermolecular forces act between separate molecules and are much weaker than bonds.
**Step 3:** London (dispersion) forces exist between all molecules and grow with molecular size.
**Step 4:** Dipole–dipole forces act between polar molecules (e.g. HCl); hydrogen bonds are especially strong dipole forces when H is bonded to N, O or F (e.g. H₂O, NH₃, HF).
**Step 5:** Stronger intermolecular forces → higher melting and boiling points.
**Example:** Water (M = 18) boils at 100 °C while hydrogen sulphide H₂S (M = 34) boils at −60 °C: water molecules are held by hydrogen bonds, H₂S molecules only by weaker dipole and London forces.

cards.title: Mnemonic — "Hydrogen bonds need F-O-N"

cards.title: Exam tip
body: Boiling a molecular substance breaks intermolecular forces, not covalent bonds. Say this clearly in explanation questions.

*   The Hydrogen ion ($$\text{H}^+$$) has an empty $$1s$$ orbital.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following properties of metals is directly caused by the high mobility of valence electrons in metallic bonding?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Recall metallic bonding model**
Metals consist of a lattice of positive metal cations immersed in a highly mobile, delocalized 'sea' of valence electrons.

**Step 2: Connect electron mobility to physical properties**
Because these delocalized electrons can move freely under an applied electrical voltage, metals show **high electrical conductivity**.

**Step 3: Final Answer**
The correct property is **High electrical conductivity**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: All are **intramolecular** force of attraction except:
cards.why: **Intramolecular forces** are the bonds that hold atoms together *within* a molecule (Ionic, Covalent, Metallic). **Ion-dipole** is an *intermolecular* force, which acts *between* an ion and a polar molecule (like salt dissolving in water).

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which substance has hydrogen bonding between its molecules?
cards.why:
**Step 1:** Hydrogen bonds form when H is bonded directly to a very electronegative atom: N, O or F.

**Step 2:** NH₃ has N–H bonds → hydrogen bonding.

**Step 3:** CH₄ (C–H), H₂S (S–H) and HCl (Cl–H) do not meet the F-O-N condition.

**Tip:** Hydrogen bonding explains the high boiling points of H₂O, NH₃ and HF.

cards.title: 2.2.2 Covalent Bonding
body: By sharing a single pair, two pairs and three pairs of electrons; single, double and triple bonds can be formed respectively.
The melting and boiling points of ionic compounds are usually very high.
Covalent compounds melt and boil at much lower temperatures than ionic compounds do.

cards.title: 2.2.3 Polar and Non polar Covalent Bonds
body: A **Polar covalent bond** is a covalent bond in which the electrons are not equally shared.
The more electronegative atom attracts the shared electron pairs more than the one with less electronegative value.
The Cl atom has the higher electronegativity so the electrons are drawn more towards the Cl atom and away from the H atom.
Since electrons carry a negative charge, this gives the Cl atom a partial negative charge.

cards.title: From polar bonds to polar molecules, step by step
body: A **polar bond** has a partly negative end (δ−) and a partly positive end (δ+) because the two atoms have different **electronegativities**. A **polar molecule** has a δ− side and a δ+ side **overall**. A molecule can contain polar bonds and still be non-polar — the **shape** decides.

**Step 1 — Compare electronegativities (EN) for each bond.** ΔEN ≈ 0 → non-polar covalent bond (H–H, Cl–Cl, C–H is nearly non-polar). Small to moderate ΔEN → polar covalent bond (H–Cl, O–H, C=O). Large ΔEN (about 1.7–2 or more) → ionic bond (Na⁺Cl⁻). The change is gradual (textbook Fig 2.2).
**Step 2 — Draw each bond dipole** as an arrow from δ+ towards δ− (towards the more electronegative atom).
**Step 3 — Work out the shape.** Count the bonding pairs and lone pairs on the central atom: CO₂ linear, H₂O bent, NH₃ pyramidal, CH₄ and CCl₄ tetrahedral, BF₃ trigonal planar.
**Step 4 — Add the arrows.** If the shape is **symmetrical** and all outer atoms are the same, the bond dipoles cancel → **non-polar molecule**. If not, they leave a net dipole → **polar molecule**.
The textbook explains bond polarity (2.2.3); deciding the polarity of a whole molecule from its shape is added here because exam questions ask it.
**Shortcut:** a **lone pair on the central atom** (H₂O, NH₃, SO₂) almost always makes the molecule polar; symmetrical molecules with identical outer atoms (CO₂, CH₄, CCl₄, BF₃) are non-polar.

cards.title: Model: polar and non-polar molecules

steps.text: **HCl** — one polar bond, nothing to cancel it → **polar** molecule. Cl is δ−, H is δ+.
**H₂O** — two polar O–H bonds in a **bent** shape (104.5°). The arrows both point up towards O and add → **polar**.
**CO₂** — two polar C=O bonds, but the molecule is **linear**: equal arrows point in opposite directions and cancel → **non-polar**.
**CH₄** — four C–H bonds in a symmetrical **tetrahedron**; the small dipoles cancel → **non-polar**.

body: Tap each molecule: the arrows show the bond dipoles.

cards.title: How polarity shows up in real life
body: **Charged rod test:** hold a rubbed plastic ruler near a thin stream of water — the stream **bends** towards it (polar). A stream of hexane or CCl₄ does not bend (non-polar).
**“Like dissolves like”:** polar and ionic substances dissolve in polar water (salt, sugar, ethanol); non-polar substances dissolve in non-polar solvents (grease and oil in kerosene).
**Boiling points:** for molecules of similar size, polar molecules have **higher** boiling points because dipole–dipole attractions add to London forces.

cards.title: Worked example: is NH₃ polar? is CCl₄ polar?
cards.problem: Decide whether ammonia, NH₃, and carbon tetrachloride, CCl₄, are polar molecules.

steps.text: NH₃: N (EN 3.0) is more electronegative than H (2.1) → three polar N–H bonds, N is δ−.
N has 3 bonding pairs + 1 lone pair → trigonal **pyramidal**, not symmetrical.
The three dipoles all point up towards N and do not cancel → NH₃ is **polar**.
CCl₄: Cl (3.0) is more electronegative than C (2.5) → four polar C–Cl bonds.
C has 4 bonding pairs, no lone pair → regular **tetrahedron** with four identical outer atoms.
The four dipoles cancel exactly → CCl₄ is **non-polar** (even though every bond is polar).

cards.answer: NH₃ polar (pyramidal, lone pair); CCl₄ non-polar (symmetrical tetrahedron).

cards.title: Worked example: CO₂ vs SO₂
cards.problem: CO₂ is non-polar but SO₂ is polar, although both have two polar bonds to oxygen. Explain.

steps.text: Both have polar bonds: O is more electronegative than C and than S.
CO₂: C has no lone pair → **linear** O=C=O; the two dipoles are equal and opposite → cancel.
SO₂: S has a lone pair → **bent** shape; the two dipoles point partly the same way → net dipole.

cards.answer: Shape decides: linear CO₂ cancels, bent SO₂ does not.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which molecule is non-polar even though it contains polar bonds?
cards.why: CO₂ is linear, so its two C=O dipoles cancel. H₂O (bent) and NH₃ (pyramidal) keep a net dipole; HCl has only one bond.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: A thin stream of liquid is bent by a charged rod. The liquid is most likely …
cards.why: Only **polar** molecules are attracted to the rod. Water is polar; the other three are non-polar.

cards.title: 2.2.4 Coordinate Covalent Bonding
body: Mr Hamid usually shares dinner with his best friend, Mr Paulos, at a restaurant.
One day, Mr Hamid tried to pay the bill for the dinner.
On another occasion, Mr Hamid received a good sum of money from his job and thus he invited his friend and both shared a dinner together.
The arrow points from the atom donating the lone pair to the atom accepting it.

cards.title: 2.2.5 Metallic bonding, step by step
body: **Metallic bonding** is the attraction between **positive metal ions** and the **delocalised (free-moving) valence electrons** around them. It holds metals together in the solid.
**Step 1 — Metal atoms lose their valence electrons easily** (low ionisation energy). Sodium gives 1 electron per atom, magnesium 2, aluminium 3.
**Step 2 — The atoms become positive ions (cations)** packed in regular layers (a lattice).
**Step 3 — The released electrons are delocalised:** they do not belong to one atom or one bond; they move freely through the whole metal, like a “sea” of electrons.
**Step 4 — The bond:** every cation is attracted to the electron sea and the sea is attracted to every cation. This attraction acts in **all directions**, so the bond is **non-directional**.

**What makes it stronger?** More delocalised electrons per atom, a higher ion charge and a smaller ion → stronger attraction → higher melting point. Example: Na (1 e⁻) melts at 98 °C, Mg (2 e⁻) at 650 °C, Al (3 e⁻) at 660 °C.

**Note on the textbook model (Fig. 2.3):** the circles labelled “positive nucleus” are really **positive metal ions** — each is a nucleus **plus its inner electrons**; only the valence electrons are in the sea.

cards.title: Model: the electron sea and why metals bend

states.label: Electron sea
states.text: Cations in layers, valence electrons free to move everywhere between them.

states.label: Hammered
states.text: A force slides the layers over each other. The electron sea moves with them and still holds every ion, so the metal bends instead of breaking → **malleable** and **ductile**.

cards.title: Worked example: melting points of Na, Mg, Al
cards.problem: Explain why the melting point rises from sodium (98 °C) to magnesium (650 °C) and aluminium (660 °C).

steps.text: Na gives **1**, Mg **2** and Al **3** delocalised electrons per atom.
The ions also become more highly charged (Na⁺, Mg²⁺, Al³⁺) and smaller.
More electrons in the sea + higher charge + smaller ions → stronger attraction between ions and electrons.
More energy is needed to loosen the lattice → higher melting point.

cards.answer: The metallic bond gets stronger from Na to Al.

cards.title: Worked example: why a metal conducts but solid salt does not
cards.problem: Copper conducts electricity as a solid; sodium chloride conducts only when molten or dissolved. Explain.

steps.text: A current needs **charged particles that can move**.
In copper the delocalised electrons are free to move even in the solid → conducts.
In solid NaCl the ions are locked in the lattice and there are no free electrons → no current.
When NaCl melts or dissolves, the ions become free to move → conducts.

cards.answer: Metals have mobile electrons; ionic solids have fixed ions.

cards.title: Worked example: hammering a metal and a salt
cards.problem: Why does a piece of copper flatten when hammered, while a crystal of salt shatters?

steps.text: In copper, the layers of Cu²⁺ ions slide over each other; the electron sea still surrounds every ion, so the bond is not broken → it flattens.
In NaCl, a slight shift brings ions of the **same charge** next to each other (+ next to +, − next to −).
The like charges repel and the crystal splits → brittle.

cards.answer: Metallic bonding is non-directional; ionic lattices break when like charges meet.

cards.q: Metallic bonding is the attraction between …

options.B: two nuclei and a shared pair
options.C: positive metal ions and delocalised electrons

cards.why: Metal atoms release their valence electrons; the cations are held by the sea of delocalised electrons.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which property of metals is NOT explained by delocalised electrons?
cards.why: Conductivity, lustre and malleability all come from the mobile electron sea. Density depends on how heavy and how closely packed the atoms are.

cards.title: Tips and common mistakes
body: Say “delocalised electrons”, not “free ions”: in a solid metal it is the **electrons** that move.
Metals are held by cations + electrons, not by positive and negative ions.
More valence electrons per atom → stronger metallic bond.

cards.q: Which of the following forces operates *within* a molecule to hold its constituent atoms together and is classified as a chemical bond?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Define force types**
Forces that operate *within* a molecule to hold its atoms together are chemical bonds, classified as **intramolecular forces**.

**Step 2: Compare with other options**
Intermolecular forces (like dipole-dipole and London dispersion) operate *between* separate molecules.

**Step 3: Final Answer**
The correct option is **Intramolecular force**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The dative (coordinate covalent) bond in the Ammonium ion ($$\text{NH}_4^+$$) is formed when Ammonia ($$\text{NH}_3$$) reacts with a Hydrogen ion ($$\text{H}^+$$). Which species acts as the electron pair donor?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Understand coordinate covalent bond requirements**
A dative bond requires an electron pair donor (with a lone pair) and an acceptor (with an empty orbital).

**Step 2: Analyze the reactants**
*   Ammonia ($$\text{NH}_3$$) has a non-bonding lone pair of electrons on the Nitrogen atom.
*   The Hydrogen ion ($$\text{H}^+$$) has an empty $$1s$$ orbital.
Therefore, $$\text{NH}_3$$ acts as the electron pair donor.

**Step 3: Final Answer**
The donor species is **Ammonia ($$\text{NH}_3$$)**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following pairs do **not** form a dative covalent bond to each other?
cards.why:
A **dative (coordinate) covalent bond** forms when one atom provides both electrons for the bond.
- $$ NH_3 $$ and $$ BF_3 $$ form a dative bond (N donates its lone pair to B).
- $$ NH_3 $$ and $$ H^+ $$ form $$ NH_4^+ $$ (N donates lone pair to $$ H^+ $$).
- $$ H_2O $$ and $$ H^+ $$ form $$ H_3O^+ $$ (O donates lone pair to $$ H^+ $$).
- **$$ NH_3 $$ and $$ NH_3 $$** interact via **Hydrogen bonding**, not dative covalent bonding.

cards.title: Exam question, solved
cards.problem: Which of the following diatomic molecules is formed by **sharing two pairs** of electrons?  A) $$ Cl_2 $$  B) $$ O_2 $$  C) $$ N_2 $$  D) $$ F_2 $$  E) $$ H_2 $$

steps.text:
**Step 1.** Sharing electron pairs forms covalent bonds:
- **Single bond:** 1 pair shared (e.g., $$ H_2, Cl_2, F_2 $$).
- **Double bond:** 2 pairs shared (e.g., $$ O_2 $$).
- **Triple bond:** 3 pairs shared (e.g., $$ N_2 $$).

**Step 2.** Oxygen ($$ O $$) has 6 valence electrons and needs 2 more to complete its octet, thus sharing 2 pairs with another Oxygen atom.

**Result:** B

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following bonds is classified as a polar covalent bond based on electronegativity values? (EN values: $$\text{H} = 2.1$$, $$\text{Cl} = 3.0$$, $$\text{O} = 3.5$$, $$\text{Na} = 0.9$$, $$\text{F} = 4.0$$)
cards.why:
**Step 1: Calculate electronegativity differences ($$\Delta\text{EN}$$) for the options**
*   For $$\text{H}_2$$: $$\Delta\text{EN} = 2.1 - 2.1 = 0.0$$ (Nonpolar covalent)
*   For $$\text{NaCl}$$: $$\Delta\text{EN} = 3.0 - 0.9 = 2.1$$ (Ionic, since $$> 1.8$$)
*   For $$\text{HCl}$$: $$\Delta\text{EN} = 3.0 - 2.1 = 0.9$$ (Polar covalent, since $$0.4 \le \Delta\text{EN} \le 1.8$$)
*   For $$\text{NaF}$$: $$\Delta\text{EN} = 4.0 - 0.9 = 3.1$$ (Ionic)

**Step 2: Conclusion**
Therefore, the polar covalent bond is in **$$\text{HCl}$$**.

cards.title: 2.3 Intermolecular Forces of Attraction
body: The positive and negative poles of the polar liquid attract the negative and positive ions of the ionic substance, respectively.
The strength of these interactions depends on the charge and the size of the ion and on the magnitude of polarity and size of the dipole.
Dipole-Dipole forces These forces occur when polar molecules arrange themselves such that their oppositely charged ends can attract each other.
The hydrogen atom has a slightly positive charge and the chlorine atom has a slightly negative charge.
Because of the force of attraction between oppositely charged particles, there is a small dipole-dipole force of attraction between adjacent HCl molecules.

cards.title: Intermolecular Forces of Attraction
body: Between molecules: weak intermolecular forces (including hydrogen bonding in water, which is why water is liquid and has a high boiling point for such a small molecule).

cards.title: London (dispersion) forces, step by step
body: London forces (dispersion forces) are the **weakest** intermolecular forces, but they act between **all** molecules and atoms — and they are the **only** attraction between non-polar molecules and noble-gas atoms.
**Step 1 — Electrons move.** In a non-polar molecule the electron cloud is evenly spread *on average*, but at any instant it may be a little more on one side.
**Step 2 — Instantaneous dipole.** For that instant the molecule has a δ− side and a δ+ side.
**Step 3 — Induced dipole.** That tiny dipole pushes or pulls the electrons of the neighbouring molecule, creating a dipole in it, lined up so that δ+ faces δ−.
**Step 4 — Attraction.** The two short-lived dipoles attract. Millions of these flickering attractions together hold the molecules (Fig 2.10: two iodine molecules).

**What makes them stronger?** (1) **More electrons / bigger molecules** — a large electron cloud is easily distorted (more polarisable). (2) **Larger contact area** — long, straight molecules touch more than compact, round ones.

cards.title: Model: how a London force forms

states.label: Even cloud
states.text: Two non-polar molecules; on average the electrons are spread evenly — no dipole.

states.label: Instant dipole
states.text: Electrons drift to one side of the left molecule: δ− on one side, δ+ on the other.

states.label: Induced dipole
states.text: The δ+ end attracts the electrons of the right molecule → an induced dipole. δ+ … δ− attraction = London force.

body: Slide to see the three stages.

cards.title: Memory trick
body: **“Big clouds wobble more.”** More electrons → a bigger, softer cloud → easier to distort → stronger London forces → higher boiling point.

cards.title: Worked example: why is I₂ a solid but Cl₂ a gas?
cards.problem: Chlorine is a gas and iodine a solid at room temperature, yet both are non-polar X₂ molecules. Explain.

steps.text: Both molecules are non-polar, so the only forces between molecules are **London forces**.
I₂ has 106 electrons; Cl₂ has 34. I₂ has the much larger electron cloud.
A larger cloud is more easily distorted → bigger instantaneous dipoles → stronger London forces.
More energy is needed to separate I₂ molecules → higher melting and boiling points → solid at 25 °C.

cards.answer: Stronger London forces between the larger I₂ molecules.

cards.title: Worked example: HCl vs F₂
cards.problem: HCl (M = 36.5) boils at −85 °C; F₂ (M = 38) boils at −188 °C. Why the big difference for molecules of similar mass?

steps.text: Similar mass and number of electrons → similar London forces.
F₂ is non-polar: London forces only.
HCl is polar: London forces **plus dipole–dipole** attractions.
Extra attraction → more energy needed to boil → HCl has the higher boiling point.

cards.answer: HCl has dipole–dipole forces in addition to London forces.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which noble gas has the highest boiling point?
cards.why: Xe has the most electrons → strongest London forces → highest boiling point.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The only intermolecular force between CH₄ molecules is …
cards.why: CH₄ is non-polar and has no H on N, O or F, so only London forces act.

cards.title: Tips and common mistakes
body: Polar **bonds** ≠ polar **molecule**: always check the shape.
London forces are present in **every** molecular substance — even polar ones. They are not “only for non-polar molecules”; they are just the *only* force there.
Compare boiling points in this order: first check for hydrogen bonding, then polarity, then size (electrons).

cards.title: Mnemonic
body: Ionic = I own it (transfer). Covalent = co-own (share). Metallic = mobile sea. “Giant covalent does not dissolve and does not melt easily.”

cards.title: How to classify an unknown solid
body: Ask four school tests: melting point high or low? Does the solid conduct? Does the melt/solution conduct? Does it dissolve in water? High melt + conducts only when molten/dissolved → ionic. High melt + never conducts + insoluble → giant covalent. Low melt + never conducts → simple molecular. Conducts as a solid and bends → metal.

Dot-and-cross: metals lose until they look noble; non-metals gain or share until they look noble. MgCl₂ needs two Cl because Mg gives two electrons. Covalent pairs sit between symbols; leftover dots are lone pairs. Lone pairs push — that is why water is bent and ammonia is pyramidal (named properly in Grade 12).

Hydrogen bonding is a special strong intermolecular force, not a fourth primary bond. It explains water’s high boiling point, ice floating, and DNA later. When water boils you break H-bonds between molecules, not the O–H covalent bonds inside a molecule — if you broke those you would make hydrogen and oxygen gases.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following substances consists of completely nonpolar covalent bonds?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Identify bond type of homonuclear diatomic molecules**
Homonuclear diatomic molecules contain two identical nonmetal atoms.

**Step 2: Apply electronegativity values**
For $$\text{Cl}_2$$, the electronegativity difference is:
$$\Delta\text{EN} = \text{EN of Cl} - \text{EN of Cl} = 3.0 - 3.0 = 0.0$$
Since the sharing of electrons is perfectly equal, the bonds are entirely nonpolar covalent.

**Step 3: Final Answer**
The nonpolar covalent substance is **$$\text{Cl}_2$$**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following lists intermolecular forces in the correct order of increasing attractive strength?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Compare relative strengths of intermolecular forces**
*   London dispersion forces (caused by temporary fluctuations in electron clouds) are the weakest.
*   Dipole-dipole forces (between permanent polar molecules) are of intermediate strength.
*   Hydrogen bonding (a exceptionally strong, unique dipole-dipole attraction involving FON) is the strongest of these three.

**Step 2: Final Answer**
The correct increasing order is **London dispersion < dipole-dipole < Hydrogen bonding**.

glossary.meaning: Metallic bonding refers to the interaction between the delocalized electrons and the positive metal ions.
A Polar covalent bond is a covalent bond in which the electrons are not equally shared.
Electronegativity is the attractive power of an atom for shared electron pairs.
A molecule with an overall δ+ end and δ− end because its bond dipoles do not cancel.
Weak attractions between instantaneous and induced dipoles; present between all molecules.
Valence electrons that are not tied to one atom or bond but move freely through the whole structure (as in metals).

tips.text: Covalent bonds are formed by the sharing of electrons, which commonly occurs when two nonmetals bond together.
A coordinate covalent bond, also called a dative bond, is a force of attraction resulting from the sharing of a lone pair of electrons from one atom with another atom.
Metallic bonding refers to the interaction between the delocalized electrons and the positive metal ions.

The physical properties of metals, electrical conductivity, high melting and boiling point, lustre, malleability and ductility are mainly due to the delocalized electrons. These attractive forces occur when an ionic substance dissolves in a polar liquid, e.g.
The positive and negative poles of the polar liquid attract the negative and positive ions of the ionic substance, respectively.

questions.q: Explain, step by step, how London forces arise between two non-polar molecules.
questions.answer: Electrons move, so for an instant one molecule has an uneven cloud (instantaneous dipole); this distorts the neighbour’s cloud (induced dipole); the δ+ and δ− of the two dipoles attract.
why: Step 1: random electron movement → instantaneous dipole.
Step 2: it induces a dipole in a neighbouring molecule.
Step 3: the opposite partial charges attract — a London force.
Step 4: the dipoles keep changing, so the force is weak and short-lived.
questions.tip: Key words: instantaneous dipole, induced dipole, attraction.

similar.q: Why do London forces increase with molecular size?

questions.q: Give two differences between metallic bonding and ionic bonding.

Step 2: compare a property: conduction in the solid (no vs yes).
